issues.legal_issue: A land-ceiling scheme that uses an artificial definition of family and different ceiling treatment for members of natural families violates equal protection when it discriminates between similarly situated persons.
material_facts: The law fixed the same ceiling for an individual and a defined family of up to five members, with a different ceiling for larger defined families.
Its definition of family excluded some members of natural families recognized under personal law, including major sons in the example considered by the Court.
Applying the definition and ceiling could leave members of the same natural family with materially different amounts of land, without justification for that difference.
issues.conclusion: The ceiling provision violated Article 14, and because it was the basis of the chapter on fixation of ceiling, that entire chapter had to fall.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits discrimination between persons equally circumstanced. Following Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala, an artificial family definition combined with different ceiling standards may produce unconstitutional discrimination. The Court noted that the law was not protected by Article 31-A.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: Persons brought a constitutional challenge to a law that imposed limits on land holdings.
predicates.artificial_family_definition: The law defined a family in a way that did not correspond to natural families recognized under personal law.
predicates.unequal_burdens_within_natural_families: Applying the family definition and ceiling left members of the same natural family with different land burdens, without an identified justification.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling law is challenged, an artificial family definition that produces unequal burdens within natural families means the ceiling scheme violates equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation scheme that progressively reduces effective compensation as the landholder's net income increases violates equal protection when it discriminates between similarly situated persons.
material_facts: The law calculated compensation for acquired land using successive slabs of net annual income and lower multipliers for later slabs.
The resulting effective reduction in compensation increased as total net annual income increased.

The Court found the scheme's effect comparable to the discriminatory progressive cuts considered in Karimbil Kunhikoman; the State's comparison to higher income-tax rates on higher income slabs had already been rejected in that case.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits discriminatory treatment of similarly situated persons. The Court followed Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala, which rejected justification of progressive reductions in compensation by analogy to higher income-tax rates on higher income slabs. The law was not protected by Article 31-A.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: Persons brought a constitutional challenge to a scheme for compensating landholders for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_uses_progressively_lower_mu: The scheme applied lower multipliers to successive higher slabs of a landholder's net income.
predicates.effective_compensation_cut_increases_wit: The scheme's effective reduction in total compensation grew as a landholder's net income increased.

issues.definition: When a compensation scheme is challenged, progressively lower multipliers that make the effective cut increase with income mean the scheme violates equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: An entire law must be struck down when its unconstitutional ceiling and compensation mechanisms are pivotal provisions on which the law's operation depends.
material_facts: The law's operation depended on its provisions fixing the ceiling on land holdings and determining compensation for acquired land.
The Court found both mechanisms discriminatory and unconstitutional.
The ceiling and compensation provisions were pivotal to the law's operation.
issues.conclusion: The entire law had to be struck down as unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that when pivotal provisions are unconstitutional and the working of the entire law depends on them, the whole law must fall. It treated the ceiling and compensation provisions as essential to the law's operation after holding them violative of Article 14.
